strengths: Clear problem formulation with well-defined fingerprinting requirements (reliability, persistence, stealthiness, harmlessness, robustness) that provide a principled framework
Elegant core insight that restricting watermarks to specific domains naturally improves quality preservation and durability against finetuning—simple but effective

Comprehensive evaluation covering multiple critical dimensions: perfect detection within 10-100 queries, persistence through diverse finetuning scenarios, robustness to system prompts, and preservation of out-of-domain quality

Strong empirical results with statistical guarantees: achieves detection with p < 1e-5 across settings, and monotonicity enables recovery even after adversarial finetuning via additional queries (~$1 for 1000 queries)
Thorough comparisons with backdoor-based methods (instructional and scalable fingerprints), showing superiority across all key requirements—first systematic comparison of these approaches
Extensive evaluation against existing watermarking baselines (KGW-D) demonstrating 6% PPL improvement, clearer domain confinement (TPR@1%), and successful persistence where alternatives fail
Extensive appendices with valuable ablations (hyperparameter sensitivity), domain versatility studies (tokens, multiple keys, harmful content), domain leakage analysis, and reproducibility details
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily combines existing techniques (KGW watermarks [23] + logit distillation [17] + domain-specific training). Algorithm 2 is straightforward—matching logit distributions on target domain while regularizing on general domain. Core contribution is application rather than methodology

Domain selection problem critically underexplored: Appendix C.3 reveals that 10%+ domain contamination significantly degrades performance; different domains show disparate capacity (Math: poor, French/Health: good); in-domain quality suffers substantially (PPL: 3.33→11.5 for French). No principled guidance provided despite acknowledged practical importance

Incomplete threat model: assumes provider can query API freely in target domain; doesn't evaluate adaptive adversaries who know the scheme or perform selective finetuning on suspected domains. If domain is revealed, targeted finetuning trivially removes watermarks (Fig. 3). No evaluation of watermark removal via distillation/pruning

Arbitrary statistical decisions: choice of α = 1e-5 lacks justification; no analysis of false positives when natural queries cluster in certain domains; monotonicity exploitation requires thousands of queries, but cost/time tradeoffs in realistic deployment not discussed

Evaluation scope too narrow: only 2 base models (primarily small), only 3 main domains, no evaluation of watermark removal attacks or adversarial finetuning with model knowledge. Comparisons with recent watermarking approaches [16, 19, 24] are superficial

Quality-watermark tradeoff inadequately addressed: substantial in-domain PPL increases (3.33→11.5) could be detectable artifacts that compromise stealthiness claims. Paper doesn't discuss whether quality differences themselves fingerprint the model

Multi-watermark scalability severely limited: Appendix C.2 shows 4 watermarks reduce TPR@1% to ~50% with key confusion. Undermines applicability to multi-party fingerprinting scenarios mentioned as 'promising future direction'

Stealthiness claims overstated: fingerprints are stealth only if adversary doesn't know the queried domain; a knowledgeable adversary could monitor or block domain-specific queries. Calling them 'inherently stealth' is misleading given threat model

Practical guidance insufficient: no principled method for domain selection, no guidance on detecting domain leakage, no analysis of entropy requirements for different domains, no real-world deployment case study

Regulatory/legal considerations absent: paper focuses on technical soundness but doesn't discuss licensing enforcement via fingerprinting in real-world contexts where legal proof standards may differ from statistical guarantees

strengths: Well-motivated approach to an important practical problem: addresses limitations of existing OSM watermarks (quality degradation and brittleness to finetuning) with intuitive domain-specific constraints

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple dimensions (reliability, persistence, robustness, stealthiness) with strong results on controlled metrics (~10-100 queries for detection, quality preservation outside target domain)

Thorough experimental work with extensive ablations (hyperparameters, multiple domains, multiple models) and honest comparisons with instructional and scalable fingerprinting baselines showing clear tradeoffs
Clear presentation with well-designed algorithms and figures; good use of statistical testing framework with controlled false positive rates
Careful attention to practical deployment scenarios including system prompts and multiple finetuning settings
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: core contribution is applying domain-specific constraints to existing KGW watermark distillation (Gu et al. 2024), which is a relatively straightforward incremental advance for a top-tier venue

Unresolved domain selection problem: Appendix C.3 shows that 10% domain overlap between training and regularization datasets significantly degrades performance, yet the paper provides no principled framework for practitioners to select watermark domains despite acknowledging 'ensuring no domain overlap is challenging'

Critical domain-dependent variability in persistence: Table 3 shows Math domain achieves only 50% detection accuracy even with 1000 queries when finetuned in-domain, while French remains perfect, indicating extreme sensitivity to domain choice without principled solutions

Incomplete threat model and adversarial analysis: assumes passive observation only; does not evaluate against (1) active adversaries who detect query patterns from 100+ domain-specific queries, (2) watermark removal attacks (distillation, targeted finetuning), or (3) adversaries who finetune specifically on the watermark domain

Stealthiness claim relies on single example (Fig. 5) without systematic evidence; an adversary observing 100+ math queries all generating watermarked text would detect the fingerprinting attempt despite individual queries appearing natural

Limited evaluation scope: only two model sizes with instruction-tuning; no base models; no evaluation of watermark removal attacks or adaptive adversaries; multiple watermark keys show significant confusion (Appendix C.2) limiting scalability

Critical practical limitations relegated to appendices: domain leakage analysis (C.3), multiple key confusion (C.2), and hyperparameter sensitivity (B) are foundational issues that should be prominently discussed with solutions for top-tier publication

Weak theoretical justification: no formal analysis of why domain specificity improves persistence; regularization loss (Eq. 4) lacks principled justification beyond intuition; no theoretical guarantees or bounds provided
Hyperparameter selection guidance missing: Appendix B shows sensitivity to h and δ parameters but paper provides no principled approach for practitioners to tune these for new domains

Under-specified for practical deployment: no systematic guidance on domain selection when boundaries are fuzzy; no evaluation of whether watermark domain can be inferred by adversaries; no discussion of computational costs compared to alternatives

strengths: Well-articulated fingerprinting requirements framework clearly identifying why existing methods fail
Elegant core insight that restricting watermarks to specific domains improves durability and quality while maintaining statistical guarantees
Exceptionally comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple models, domains, and deployment scenarios with clear improvements over baselines on all criteria
Strong empirical results showing perfect detection within 10-200 queries with robustness to system prompts and natural stealthiness
Thorough experimental validation including detailed comparisons with instructional fingerprints and scalable fingerprints demonstrating superiority across all requirements
Properly leverages statistical testing framework to provide formal false positive rate control and detection power scaling
Excellent presentation with clear motivation, effective figures, and thorough appendices including ablations and broader impact discussion
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty as the approach primarily combines existing KGW watermarking and logit distillation with domain restriction being the main new contribution

Critical practical limitation revealed in Section C.3: even 5-10% domain leakage significantly degrades watermark specificity, and authors acknowledge clean domain separation is 'challenging' in real-world settings with no proposed solutions
Persistence degrades substantially when adversary finetunes on the target domain, requiring 1000 queries for recovery with unclear detectability and API cost assumptions that may not generalize
Evaluation limited to 1B and 7B models with no testing on larger models (70B+) where watermark signals may scale differently or become harder to detect
Scalability to multiple watermarks is weak with TPR dropping to ~50% at 1% FPR with 4 keys and acknowledged cross-contamination issues
Stealthiness evaluation is incomplete with only one example shown and no quantitative assessment of adversarial detectability of domain-specific query patterns
Domain selection guidance is lacking with no clear principles for practitioners and significant performance variance across domains (Math particularly weak)
Missing statistical details including confidence intervals, number of random seeds, and justification for threshold choices
Incomplete threat model analysis lacking discussion of adaptive adversaries, query rate limiting, domain-blocking defenses, and scenarios with partial domain contamination

strengths: Novel and well-motivated paradigm: The shift from query-key pairs to semantic domains + statistical signals is conceptually sound and addresses fundamental limitations of prior work. Clear motivation in Section 3.1.

Exceptional experimental rigor: Comprehensive evaluation across 25+ deployment scenarios, 5 targeted adversarial attacks, multiple models and domains. 100% FSR across all scenarios is a substantial improvement.
Strong technical foundation: Theorem D.1 properly grounds the Z-test; regularization loss is well-motivated; Algorithm 1 is clear. Sound mathematical framework.
First method achieving both robustness and stealth: Robust to finetuning, quantization, pruning, and system prompts while remaining undetectable to generic adversaries. This is a genuine advance.
Principled stealth evaluation: Using GPT5-MINI as a judge to assess detectability is novel and convincing. Results show ~0% recall on queries and ~10% on outputs.
Thorough ablations: Systematic examination of design choices (number of queries, semantic domain, watermark strength, regularization) across multiple appendices.
Excellent reproducibility: Code provided, comprehensive hyperparameter details, datasets documented, environment specification included.
weaknesses: Limited component-level novelty: Individual components (Red-Green watermark, distillation) are from prior work. The contribution is primarily in their combination, making this more of an engineering contribution than a fundamental advance.

Semantic domain selection under-explored: No principled guidance for domain selection; assumes adversaries don't know the domain (critical assumption relegated to brief limitations discussion); missing analysis of domain discovery scenarios or overlaps with user queries.

Quality degradation on semantic domain: Table 4 shows 30% drop in LLM-as-judge scores on French domain. While not affecting benchmarks, this degrades user experience and could reveal the fingerprint through quality inconsistencies.

Detection cost not fully addressed: Requires 1000 queries (~$0.20 per detection). Missing analysis of rate-limiting, query monitoring, or whether frequent detection attempts could themselves reveal fingerprinting.

Limited baseline strength: IF and SF use supervised finetuning while the proposed method uses watermark distillation—different training paradigms. Baselines might be stronger if trained with similar techniques.

Incomplete adversarial analysis: Anti-watermark paraphraser only tested in appendix; adaptive adversaries using adversarial training to remove watermarks not explored; Figure 3 shows signal degradation but recovery with 50+ queries not analyzed.
Stealth depends on domain secrecy: If semantic domain is discovered, stealth is lost. Paper dismisses this as 'significant cost for adversary' without empirical demonstration.

Limited model coverage: Only 1B-8B models; unclear if results scale to 70B+. Only instruction-tuned models except one completion model. English/French primarily; multilingual/specialized domain models untested.
Multiple watermark keys appear limited (Appendix E.2): Only 50% TPR@1% with 4 keys; signals degrade substantially, limiting practical multi-key applicability.
Theorem D.1 practical assumptions: Requires 'max_h m_h = o(√n_eff(ω))' for context diversity. When would this assumption violate in practice? Not discussed. Could fail for short prompts.

strengths: Clear motivation for semantic domain approach: effectively explains why query-key fingerprinting is brittle
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: extensive testing across multiple models, 25+ deployment scenarios, and various robustness settings demonstrates solid engineering
Novel technical contribution: combining semantic domain conditioning with statistical watermarking is a reasonable architectural idea
Good reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, promised code release, and clear methodology
Well-presented paper: clear writing, informative figures, and logical structure
weaknesses: Critical security assumption: entire method relies on adversaries not knowing the semantic domain. This is acknowledged only as a limitation but represents a fundamental vulnerability. Domain secrecy is unreliable (security through obscurity), and domain discovery via fine-tuning or trial-and-error is trivial

Flawed stealth evaluation: uses generic classifier unaware of semantic domain. GPT5-MINI correctly doesn't flag French text as suspicious, but this doesn't prove stealth against domain-aware adversaries who would specifically target French-domain watermarking

Weak threat model: assumes adversaries don't know the domain and don't discover it. Realistic resourced adversaries could fine-tune on the semantic domain or systematically discover which language the fingerprint uses. No defense mechanisms provided

Significant utility degradation on semantic domain: Table 4 shows ~25-38% drops in quality (GPT5 judge scores) on the semantic domain, understated in main text. Material cost for real French-language users

Unfair baseline comparisons: IF and SF use different threat models and aren't optimized for domain-based security. The paper doesn't isolate the benefit of semantic conditioning from using more queries
Non-principled domain selection: why French? No guidance for practitioners. Generalizability unclear, especially for multilingual models. Other domains tested only in appendix despite being central
Detection cost not thoroughly analyzed: 1000 queries at $0.20 may itself be detectable as suspicious activity; no analysis of rate limiting or abuse detection evasion

Inadequate analysis of semantic domain finetuning: Table 3 shows 'robustness' to finetuning on French WildChat data, but only because of 1000-query brute force accumulation, not fundamental robustness
Watermark strength parameter selection is arbitrary: δ=4 chosen without principled justification; Figure 7 reveals trade-offs but no principled selection method provided
Statistical guarantees are asymptotic: Theorem D.1 assumes N→∞, unclear if N=1000 is sufficient; assumption max_h mh = o(√neff) not empirically validated

strengths: Novel paradigm shift from fixed query-key pairs to semantic domains with statistical signals, addressing genuine limitations of prior work in both robustness and stealth
Exceptional experimental rigor: comprehensive evaluation across 25 deployment scenarios achieving 100% FSR while baselines fail repeatedly; 5 targeted adversarial scenarios; 3 model scales
Theoretically grounded detection with formal statistical guarantees (Theorem D.1) for false positive rate control via Red-Green watermarks
First quantitative stealth evaluation showing semantic domain queries achieve <1% detection vs. ~95% for Instructional Fingerprinting
Excellent presentation, clarity, and reproducibility with code, detailed hyperparameters, and thorough appendices including ablations on query count, domains, and watermark strength
Principled design combining watermark distillation (Eq. 1) with careful out-of-domain preservation (Eq. 2) using well-motivated regularization
Honest discussion of limitations including domain discovery risk, quality-utility tradeoffs, and detection costs
weaknesses: Semantic domain is a critical security assumption but receives limited formal analysis: no systematic evaluation of domain discoverability, adaptive adversary strategies, or cross-domain leakage that could reveal the watermarked domain to adversaries

Quality-utility tradeoff on semantic domain is concerning: GPT-4 judge scores drop ~30% on semantic domain (e.g., 6.90→4.82), while perplexity increases; impact on real-world usage is unclear and mitigation strategies limited

Detection cost substantially higher (1000 queries, ~$0.20) compared to Instructional Fingerprinting (8 queries), though justified by robustness gains; comparison fairness with different detection mechanisms not fully addressed

Limited theoretical analysis: why semantic conditioning improves finetuning robustness (Figure 4) lacks formal explanation; regularization loss design (Eq. 2) not rigorously justified vs. alternatives like KL divergence
Theorem D.1 assumption of context diversity (max_h m_h = o(√n_eff)) not empirically verified on actual model outputs; impact of violations on false positive rate unknown
Multiple watermark keys degrade gracefully: 4-key scenario achieves only ~50% TPR at 1% FPR vs. >95% for single key, limiting scalability to scenarios requiring independent fingerprints
Limited model diversity: only LLaMA/Qwen architectures tested; generalization to other families unclear; only one primary semantic domain tested extensively (French)
Incomplete adversarial analysis: no experiments with adaptive adversaries probing to discover domain; no cross-domain leakage evaluation; watermark radioactivity acknowledged but not fully addressed
Hyperparameter justification incomplete: only δ ablated; choices of k=1 and γ=0.25 lack sensitivity analysis and design rationale
